questions.title: Commonest source of laboratory errors
questions.question: Most lab errors are due to:

explanations.A: Correct. The great majority of laboratory errors arise in the pre-analytical phase — everything that happens before the sample is actually measured, such as test ordering, patient identification, sample collection, labelling and transport. Studies consistently attribute roughly two-thirds of all lab errors to this stage, because it involves many manual, human-dependent steps. Reducing pre-analytical error (correct identification, correct tube, correct handling) therefore yields the biggest improvement in laboratory safety.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Analytical errors — those occurring during the actual measurement on the analyser — are now relatively uncommon because of automation and internal quality control.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Post-analytical errors (result transcription, reporting, interpretation) are a real but smaller contributor than the pre-analytical phase.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Mixing up samples is one specific example of a pre-analytical error, not the overarching category the question asks for.

questions.learning_objective: State that most laboratory errors occur in the pre-analytical phase.

questions.title: Outdated surgical technique causing a patient's death
questions.question: The surgeon used old techniques that prolonged the operation and resulted in great exhaustion of the patient, who became shocked and died on table. This case is considered:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The harm arose from the surgical conduct of the operation, not from the administration of anaesthesia, so it is not an anaesthetic error.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Professional misconduct denotes ethical or disciplinary violations (e.g. dishonesty, breach of confidentiality); using an outdated operative technique is a competence/standard-of-care failure, classified here as a surgical error.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A patient died as a direct result of substandard surgical technique, so medical responsibility clearly exists rather than being absent.
explanations.D: Correct. Using outdated techniques that needlessly prolonged the operation, exhausted the patient and led to fatal shock is a failure of surgical standard of care, i.e. a surgical error. The doctor is responsible because the outcome followed from not applying accepted current technique. Such errors fall under professional negligence when they cause harm the reasonably competent surgeon would have avoided.

questions.learning_objective: Classify harm from an outdated, prolonged operative technique as a surgical error carrying medical responsibility.

questions.title: Prescribing without checking a patient's allergy
questions.question: A doctor prescribing a drug without considering the patient's allergy is doing a:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Dichotomy (fee-splitting) is an unethical financial arrangement between doctors and has nothing to do with prescribing.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Civil negligence is a legal consequence that may follow if harm results; the act of prescribing without checking the allergy is itself categorised as a medication error.
explanations.C: Correct. Prescribing a drug without accounting for the patient's known allergy is a medication error — specifically a prescribing error — because a wrong decision is made at the ordering stage of the medication process. Checking allergies is a basic prescribing safeguard, and omitting it can cause a preventable adverse drug reaction. It is classified by the step at which it occurs (prescription) rather than by any later legal label.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Professional misconduct refers to ethical/disciplinary breaches; failing to check an allergy is a patient-safety/medication error, not a conduct offence.

questions.learning_objective: Identify prescribing without checking a known allergy as a (prescribing) medication error.

questions.title: Example of an error of omission
questions.question: Which of the following is considered an error of omission?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Giving an overdose is an act that was done wrongly — an error of commission, not omission.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Giving the wrong dose is a wrong action performed, i.e. an error of commission.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Leaving a towel (retained swab) in the abdomen is something actively done incorrectly during the operation — a commission error.
explanations.D: Correct. An error of omission is a failure to do something that should have been done. Leaving samples unlabelled is the omission of a required step (labelling), so it is the classic omission example here. Omission errors contrast with commission errors, which are wrong acts that were actually carried out.

questions.module_subject: 327 MPE > Medical Professionalism & Ethics > Patient safety
questions.learning_objective: Distinguish an error of omission (failure to act, e.g. unlabelled samples) from errors of commission.

questions.title: Which is NOT an error of commission
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT considered an error of commission?

options.B: Delay in diagnosis of a disease

explanations.A: Incorrect (it IS commission). Administering an overdose is a wrong act carried out, an error of commission.
explanations.B: Correct. A delay in diagnosis is a failure to act in time — an error of omission — so it is the one that is NOT a commission error. Errors of commission are wrong actions actually performed (overdose, wrong dose, wrong patient), whereas omission errors are failures to do something indicated. The delayed diagnosis fits the omission pattern of not doing what should have been done.
explanations.C: Incorrect (it IS commission). Giving the wrong dose is a wrong action performed.
explanations.D: Incorrect (it IS commission). Operating on the wrong patient is an active wrong act, a commission error.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise a delayed diagnosis as an omission error, not a commission error.

questions.title: Example of an error of commission
questions.question: Which of the following is considered an error of commission?

options.B: Not considering history of patient's allergy
options.C: Leaving a towel in the abdomen

explanations.A: Incorrect. Delaying an indicated operation is a failure to act in time — an error of omission.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Not considering a known allergy is a failure to perform a required check, i.e. an omission.
explanations.C: Correct. Leaving a towel (retained surgical swab) in the abdomen is a wrong act actually carried out during surgery, which is the definition of an error of commission. Commission errors are things done incorrectly, as opposed to omission errors which are things not done. A retained foreign body is the textbook operative commission error.
explanations.D: Incorrect. An unsuccessful treatment outcome is not in itself an error; a poor result can occur despite correct care and does not fit the commission category.

questions.learning_objective: Identify a retained surgical towel as an error of commission.

questions.title: Safe writing of medication orders
questions.question: Medication orders should NOT:

explanations.A: Correct. Medication orders should not contain error-prone abbreviations or unnecessary decimal points, because these are a well-recognised source of dosing mistakes (e.g. a trailing zero or an ambiguous abbreviation misread as a different drug or a tenfold dose). Safe-prescribing standards call for writing terms out in full and avoiding trailing/naked decimals. This is why the negative item — what an order should not contain — is abbreviations or decimals.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Orders must of course be written (or otherwise clearly documented); an unwritten order is unsafe, so this is not what they should avoid.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Including the medication's purpose (indication) improves safety and is encouraged, not prohibited.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Orders should always consider patient-specific information such as weight, renal function and allergies.

questions.learning_objective: State that medication orders should avoid error-prone abbreviations and decimals.

questions.title: Cause of an error of omission
questions.question: Error of omission occurs as a result of:

options.A: Drugs administered at the wrong time
options.B: Surgery performed on the wrong side of the body
options.C: Delay in performing an indicated appendectomy
options.D: Transfusion using blood cross-matched for another patient

explanations.A: Incorrect. Administering a drug at the wrong time is a wrong act performed — a commission error.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Wrong-side surgery is an active wrong act, i.e. an error of commission.
explanations.C: Correct. Delaying an indicated appendectomy is a failure to perform a needed action in time, which is the essence of an error of omission. Omission errors are failures to act (not doing what should be done), in contrast to commission errors which are wrong acts carried out. The delayed indicated operation is therefore the omission example.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Transfusing blood cross-matched for another patient is a wrong act performed, a commission error.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise a delayed indicated operation as an error of omission.

questions.title: Purpose of using the metric system in dosing
questions.question: Using the metric system in weight expression is needed to avoid:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Surgical errors relate to operative technique, not to the units used for expressing weight or dose.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Anaesthetic errors concern the conduct of anaesthesia; standardising weight units is not aimed at them specifically.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Laboratory errors are dominated by pre-analytical sample handling, not by dosing units.
explanations.D: Correct. Expressing weight and dose consistently in the metric system avoids medication errors, because mixing units (e.g. apothecary measures, teaspoons) or ambiguous notation leads to dosing mistakes. Using a single standard unit system removes conversion errors and makes orders unambiguous. Standardised metric dosing is a core medication-safety measure.

questions.learning_objective: State that standardised metric weight/dose expression avoids medication errors.

questions.title: Vagal stimulation during induction of anaesthesia
questions.question: Vagal stimulation may occur during induction of anesthesia due to:

explanations.A: Correct. During induction, instrumentation of the upper airway — laryngoscopy and tracheal intubation — stimulates the vagus and can trigger reflex bradycardia or even cardiac arrest. This airway-manipulation reflex is the induction-phase cause of vagal stimulation. Adequate depth of anaesthesia and, when needed, an anticholinergic (atropine) blunt the response.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Traction on viscera provokes vagal reflexes during the surgical/maintenance phase when the abdomen is being handled, not at induction.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Improper premedication may fail to blunt reflexes but is not itself the direct vagal stimulus asked for at induction.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Overdose of anaesthetic causes cardiorespiratory depression rather than a specific vagal (parasympathetic) reflex on airway instrumentation.

questions.title: Death from a prolonged operation
questions.question: A prolonged operation may cause death due to:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Hypoxia is an airway/ventilation problem and is not the characteristic consequence of mere prolongation of surgery.
explanations.B: Correct. A needlessly prolonged operation exhausts the patient and, through sustained tissue trauma, blood and fluid loss and pain, produces surgical (neurogenic/hypovolaemic) shock, which can be fatal. This is the mechanism highlighted in the earlier vignette of the outdated, prolonged technique that ended in fatal shock. Keeping operative time appropriate is therefore a patient-safety priority.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Hypothermia can complicate long procedures but is a contributory factor, not the single named cause the item asks for.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Cardiac arrest is a terminal event that may result from shock or hypoxia, not the specific answer for prolongation itself.

questions.title: Causes of death under anaesthesia — the exception
questions.question: Causes of death under anesthesia include all of the following, EXCEPT:

options.A: Sympathetic shock due to light anesthesia
options.D: Respiratory or myocardial depression due to anesthetic overdose

explanations.A: Correct. This is the exception because light (too-shallow) anaesthesia provokes reflexes through the PARAsympathetic (vagal) system, not the sympathetic system — so 'sympathetic shock due to light anaesthesia' is the incorrect statement. Under light anaesthesia, surgical stimulation triggers vagal reflexes that can cause bradycardia and cardiac arrest. Naming it sympathetic reverses the autonomic pathway, which is why it is the odd one out.
explanations.B: Incorrect (it IS a real cause). Obstruction of the air passage (by secretions, vomitus or foreign body) is a genuine cause of anaesthetic death.
explanations.C: Incorrect (it IS a real cause). Hypoxia is a leading mechanism of death under anaesthesia.
explanations.D: Incorrect (it IS a real cause). Anaesthetic overdose causes respiratory and myocardial depression that can be fatal.

questions.title: Airway obstruction under anaesthesia
questions.question: Obstruction of air passages under anesthesia may occur due to:

explanations.A: Incorrect as the single best answer. Bronchospasm does obstruct the airway, but it is only one of the listed mechanisms.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the single best answer. Aspirated vomitus obstructs the airway, yet it is one mechanism among several.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the single best answer. A retained piece of gauze can obstruct the airway, but again it is only one example.
explanations.D: Correct. Airway obstruction under anaesthesia can be caused by bronchospasm, by aspirated vomitus, or by a foreign body such as a piece of gauze — so all three apply and the complete answer is 'any of the above'. Because each listed item is a genuine cause, no single option is sufficient. Anticipating and clearing these is central to safe airway management.

questions.title: Death during dental surgery — the exception
questions.question: Death during the course of dental surgery may occur as a result of any of the following, EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Correct. Surgical shock (from major blood/fluid loss and prolonged operative trauma) is characteristic of major surgery, not of dental procedures, so it is the exception here. Dental-surgery deaths instead follow airway events (aspirated blood clots, an inhaled tooth) and vagal/parasympathetic reflex shock. Surgical shock is therefore the option that does not belong to the dental setting.
explanations.B: Incorrect (it IS a real cause). Aspiration of blood clots can obstruct the airway and cause death during dental work.
explanations.C: Incorrect (it IS a real cause). Parasympathetic (vagal) reflex shock can be provoked during dental manipulation and prove fatal.
explanations.D: Incorrect (it IS a real cause). Inhalation of a dislodged tooth is a classic airway cause of death in dental surgery.

questions.title: Vagal stimulation under light anaesthesia
questions.question: Under light anesthesia, vagal stimulation may occur due to:

explanations.A: Incorrect as the single best answer. Tracheal intubation does provoke vagal reflexes, but it is only one of the listed stimuli.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the single best answer. Traction on viscera triggers vagal reflexes, yet it is one mechanism among several.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the single best answer. Even suturing the skin incision can evoke vagal stimulation under too-light anaesthesia, but it is only one example.
explanations.D: Correct. When anaesthesia is too light, surgical and airway stimuli of many kinds — tracheal intubation, traction on viscera, and even suturing the skin — can all provoke vagal (parasympathetic) stimulation and reflex bradycardia. Because every listed stimulus can do so, the complete answer is 'any of the above'. Adequate anaesthetic depth and vagolytic premedication reduce this risk.
